title: Steel distributors assert they’re being stiffed on tariff rebates
html:
A plasma cutting machine fabricates steel parts at Titus Steel's distribution facility in Mississauga, Ont., causing sparks to fly. The company's application for tariff relief was turned down by the Finance Ministry.Sammy Kogan/The Globe and Mail

Canadian steel distributor Titus Steel Co. didn’t expect any pushback after it applied for tariff relief from Ottawa on imports of specialized “oil quenched” steel.

Last year, the federal government brought in tariff rate quotas (TRQs) on imported steel to help Canadian mills win more business during the trade war with the United States. The duties are designed to encourage distributors to buy steel made in this country, but not penalize them for importing steel that isn’t manufactured in Canada. Since the TRQs are levied across the board on all steel imports, the government allows distributors to claim a rebate on the tariffs if they can prove the specific product isn’t made in Canada.

Obtaining the rebate appeared to be a slam dunk for Mississauga-based Titus, since the type of steel it imported isn’t made in Canada, and the company had the paperwork to back up its claim.

“We have e-mails and letters from every Canadian mill saying you cannot buy this in Canada, and they do not make it,” Titus president Steve Usatis said in an interview.

But Titus was turned down by the Finance Ministry, the department that oversees the remission system. Mr. Usatis was informed that even though Canadian steel maker Algoma Steel Group Inc. doesn’t make the oil-quenched steel, that “one day, possibly, they might start making it.”

Titus workers operate steel cutting machines at the Mississauga facility. Compared with steelmakers, distributors and other players in the industry are getting a raw deal, company president Steve Usatis said.Sammy Kogan/The Globe and Mail

Canadian steel wholesalers say that Ottawa’s tariff remission system is broken. They claim that federal and provincial governments are disproportionately favouring domestic steelmakers over distributors during the trade war. In addition to the TRQ support, distributors point to the copious amounts of direct financial aid some steelmakers have received, such as the $500-million loan Algoma got from Ottawa and Ontario last year.

Compared with the steelmakers, the rest of the industry – including distributors and the many downstream manufacturers that purchase steel products – are getting a raw deal, Mr. Usatis said.

“Our customers in automotive, manufacturing, mining, recycling will be forced to pay 50 per cent more for the specialty steels they require to stay profitable and competitive, while not saving a single job in Canadian steelmaking because none of that steel is made in Canada,” he said.

Laura Devoni, Algoma’s vice-president of human resources and corporate affairs, wrote in an e-mail to The Globe and Mail that the company can’t speak to any individual application for tariff relief and remission decisions made by Ottawa.

She added that the Sault Ste. Marie, Ont.-based steel maker provides information to the government about the products it makes, and those it is developing, “so that remission supports genuine gaps in Canadian supply, rather than displacing Canadian production.”

Titus Steel’s frustration in obtaining what it believes is legitimate tariff relief isn’t unique.

Jim Ritchie, CEO of British Columbia-based steel distributor Cascadia Metals Ltd., has been turned down repeatedly on what he said are valid remission requests.

“There’s all kinds of stuff that isn’t made in Canada that we’re paying tariffs on,” he said. “Exemptions we’ve asked for, and we’re getting crickets from them. They don’t answer at all. That’s their passive-aggressive way, like they don’t even acknowledge that they got the e-mail. That’s how bad it is.”

For this year, countries with a free-trade agreement with Canada are allowed to export 75 per cent of 2024 steel volumes tariff-free. A 50-per-cent levy applies for levels above that. (The U.S. and Mexico are excluded.)

For countries without a free-trade deal with Canada, only 20 per cent of 2024 volumes can enter the country tariff-free, before the 50 per cent tariff kicks in.

Titus Steel owner Mike Usatis showcases small-batch, internationally imported steel parts at the Mississauga facility. Titus is not the only steel distributor that has struggled to obtain tariff relief.Sammy Kogan/The Globe and Mail

Ottawa appears to be aware that its TRQ system isn’t working the way it should, and is taking steps to address it.

John Fragos, press secretary to Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, wrote in an e-mail to The Globe that the government is allocating additional resources to respond to the high volume of TRQ remission requests, “with a view to providing relief where circumstances warrant.”

“Canadian producers are consulted to determine whether there is domestic production capacity to supply the goods in question,” Mr. Fragos wrote in his e-mail. “Where a lack of domestic production capability is identified, remission may be granted.”

Last week, the federal government made some changes. In a Nov. 17 release, Ottawa said that it is expanding remission coverage to an additional 23 steel Chinese products where “Canadian supply is insufficient or unavailable.”

But one aspect of the TRQs that isn’t accounted for is customer preferences for specific steel products from an overseas manufacturer when there are quality concerns about using Canadian steel.

Mr. Usatis points to a type of steel plate called AR500 that Algoma makes. Even though Titus can buy this product from Algoma, Mr. Usatis said one of its OEM customers, Caterpillar Inc., has specified it will not accept the Algoma-sourced product owing to what it says are quality issues. This essentially forces Titus to buy AR500 from an alternative supplier, and potentially have to pay a TRQ with no chance of obtaining a remission.

When Algoma was asked to comment on Titus raising quality concerns about its AR500 product, Ms. Devoni didn’t respond directly but said it welcomes the opportunity “to work with any Canadian distributor or manufacturer to understand their requirements.”

Caterpillar did not respond to a request for comment.
summary: Federal remission system is meant to provide relief when a distributor can prove an imported product isn’t made in Canada
